cognate: Gk ὄνομα = Ved. nā́man- = Av. nąman- = Lat. nōmen < *h₁nómn̥; Gk τίθημι (mid. τίθεμαι) = Ved. dhā- (mid. dadhe) = Av. (fra-)dā- = Lat. -dere in in-dere < *dʰeh₁- 'put, set'
drift_or_renewal: none in Greek/Indo-Iranian; Latin keeps the root only in the compound in-dere (nōmen indere), the simplex having merged into dare/-dere
shared_syntax: *h₁nómn̥ as direct object of *dʰeh₁-, often in the middle voice (Gk ἔθου, τιθεμένους, τίθενται, Hom. θῆαι/τίθεσθε; Ved. dadhé, dadhete, dádhānaḥ, dadhire): 'set (for oneself / one's own) a name' = 'give or take a name'
context: Naming: in Theages 122d Socrates praises the name the father 'set' (middle ἔθου) for his son (ὑεῖ); in RV 1.103.4 'when the son (sūnúḥ) took a name (nā́ma dadhé) for fame'; in AV 5.1.6 they 'took immortal names'; Sophist 225a and Phaedrus 267d use the same phrase for giving a name to a thing. The wider witnesses are naming a child: Od. 19.403-6 (Autolycus names his grandson Odysseus, θῆαι/τίθεσθε ὄνομα), Vd 18.52 (giving a son a name), Plautus Capt. (nomen indere). The match goes beyond 'name' plus any verb: all four branches pick the same verb root for the speech act, Greek and Vedic share the middle voice, and in Greek and Avestan the context is naming a son. Other verbs were available in every branch (καλέω, ὀνομάζω; Ved. vac-/ah-; Lat. uocare, appellare).

cognate: Gk ἐγείρω, perf. ἐγρήγορα (reduplicated) = Ved. jāgr̥- (reduplicated intensive/perfect jāgāra) = Av. fra-γrā-/jaγāurvah- < *h₁ger- 'wake'; Gk ὕπνος = Av. xᵛafna- = Ved. svápna-/svap- < *swep- 'sleep'
drift_or_renewal: Greek replaces the verb 'sleep' with καθεύδω in the Theaetetus merism but keeps *swep- in the noun ὕπνος (Lysis, Homer); Vedic wakes a sleeper with budh-, not jāgr̥-
shared_syntax: opposed pair (merism) of *h₁ger- 'be awake' and *swep- 'sleep' covering all of a person's time (Ved. yád jā́grataḥ yát svapántaḥ 'whether waking or sleeping'; Gk ὃν καθεύδομεν ᾧ ἐγρηγόραμεν 'the time we sleep and the time we are awake'), and the narrower 'wake from sleep' (abl./ἐξ + *swep-no- + participle of *h₁ger-: Gk ἐξ ὕπνου ἐγρόμενος ~ Av. xᵛafnāδa fraγrisəmnō)
context: Plato Theaet. 158c sets equal times of sleeping and waking against each other (ὕπαρ/ὄναρ); RV 10.164.3 and AV 6.96.3 confess sins done 'waking or sleeping'; Lysis 204d says of people 'waking from sleep'; HN 1.13 says of a man 'waking from sleep' who praises Aṣa. The cognate reduplicated stem *h₁ge-h₁gor- (ἐγρήγορα ~ jāgr̥-) used for the 'waking' term is the notable part. Still, a sleep/wake merism is found in all languages, and these are the ordinary words in each branch, so chance can't be excluded.

support.locus: Lucr. 1.938 and its repeat in book 4 (LASLA LucrDRN4-H-00-840)

cognate: Gk γλυκύς = Lat. dulcis < *dl̥kú-/*dléwku- 'sweet'; Gk μέλι = Lat. mel < *mélit 'honey'
drift_or_renewal: the Vedic version (RV 8.24.20, speech 'sweeter than ghee and honey') renews both terms: svā́dīyas (*swéh₂d-, = Gk ἡδίων) and mádhu (*médʰu, = Gk μέθυ 'wine')
shared_syntax: comparative of *dl̥kú- + standard of comparison *mélit in the genitive (Gk) or ablative (Lat., Ved.): γλυκίων μέλιτος ~ melle dulcior
context: Plato quotes Il. 18.109 (anger 'far sweeter than dripping honey'); Plautus Asin. 614 'melle dulci dulcior tu es' of a beloved; Lucretius 1.947 sweetens his song 'musaeo dulci melle'. The poetic use for sweet speech (Il. 1.249, Nestor's voice; Lucr. 1.947, poetry; RV 8.24.20, speech) is the congruent part. Against: 'sweeter than honey' is found in every language and these are the default words in both Greek and Latin, so the cognate pair is close to automatic.

note: Mostly Plato pivots with Cato/Lucretius/AV partners; nearly all empty. One strong match: *h1nómn̥ dʰeh1- (middle) name-giving, Gk~Ved~Av~Lat. Two low ones: sleep/wake (*h1ger-/*swep-) and sweeter-than-honey (Gk-Lat).
